topic.reason: הנושא הראשון ברשימה שעוד לא היה בשימוש, והוא בעונה לפי בנק הנושאים (אוקטובר עד פברואר). הוא לא נשען על תאריך בלוח השנה. בקטלוג יש ספר מתאים לקישור בהודעה (באנו חושך לגרש, ספר 14, נבדק היום באתר). רגישות (הנחה שלנו, לא נבדק): פחדים בלילה בישראל יכולים להתחבר גם לאזעקות ולממ״ד, ולכן הטקסט נשאר בחושך רגיל של חדר שינה ולא נוגע בזה. זו ריצת בדיקה של הסלייט מה-8.10 בצהריים, וריצת 22:00 תגבה אותה ל-versions.

voice.note: קול ברירת מחדל: 2 מתוך 15 דוגמאות מאושרות. נכתב לפי הקול המתועד ולפי העריכות של ירין מה-8.10 (פחות הסתייגויות כמו ״הרבה פעמים״, משפטים שהורים אומרים במירכאות, סדר מילים מדובר).

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital (clinical staff, updated 1 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... briefly checking in on them in their bed and reassuring them in 5 minutes, and then every 10 minutes until they are asleep. ... Avoid scary TV shows, videos, or stories that may add to your child's fears. ... a security object (like a small stuffed animal) they can keep in bed with them may be beneficial.
sources.supports: Nighttime fears are normal; do not dismiss them; a nightlight is fine; read stories about children who conquer fears; brief check-ins at 5 then 10 minutes; avoid scary media; a security object in bed.

sources.title: Helping Kids Overcome a Fear of the Dark
sources.publisher: Children's Hospital Colorado (Benjamin Mullin, PhD, 30 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: Nearly 75% of children ages 4 to 12 report having nighttime fears ... I know the dark feels scary sometimes, but I also know that you can do this ... kids need a dark environment to get adequate sleep ... one dim night light, if anything ... dimming the lights more as it reaches your child's bedtime ... Make the dark fun ... Gently guide your child back to bed ... Offer calm, confident support. ... things they've seen on TV, online or even the news
sources.supports: Nighttime fears are common at ages 4 to 12; a validating sentence; children need darkness to sleep, one dim night light at most; dim the lights through the evening; make the dark fun; calm confident return to bed; fears often come from things seen on screens.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds (Gene Beresin)
sources.quote: you can ask open ended questions like, 'What are you afraid of when you go to bed?' ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone. ... Use Books and Movies About Nighttime Fears.
sources.supports: Ask open questions about what scares the child at bedtime; praise brave steps; use books about nighttime fears.

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital (clinical staff, updated 1 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... briefly checking in on them in their bed and reassuring them in 5 minutes, and then every 10 minutes until they are asleep. ... Avoid scary TV shows, videos, or stories that may add to your child's fears. ... a security object (like a small stuffed animal) they can keep in bed with them may be beneficial.
sources.supports: Nighttime fears are normal; do not dismiss them; a nightlight is fine; read stories about children who conquer fears; brief check-ins at 5 then 10 minutes; avoid scary media; a security object in bed.

sources.title: Bedtime Fears: Helping Overcome Them
sources.publisher: Cincinnati Children's (reviewed by Anne Leopard, Child Life Specialist, Sep 2021)
sources.quote: It is normal for young children to have fears of the dark and going to bed at night. ... If he / she is afraid of monsters, don't get out the monster repellant spray or broom to sweep the monster away. ... Begin by briefly checking and reassuring in 5 minutes, then 10 minutes, then 15 minutes, then 20 minutes until your child is asleep.
sources.supports: Fear of the dark is normal in young children; skip monster spray and monster sweeping; check in at growing intervals (5, 10, 15, 20 minutes).

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds (Gene Beresin)
sources.quote: you can ask open ended questions like, 'What are you afraid of when you go to bed?' ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone. ... Use Books and Movies About Nighttime Fears.
sources.supports: Ask open questions about what scares the child at bedtime; praise brave steps; use books about nighttime fears.

sources.title: Bedtime Fears: Helping Overcome Them
sources.publisher: Cincinnati Children's (reviewed by Anne Leopard, Child Life Specialist, Sep 2021)
sources.quote: It is normal for young children to have fears of the dark and going to bed at night. ... If he / she is afraid of monsters, don't get out the monster repellant spray or broom to sweep the monster away. ... Begin by briefly checking and reassuring in 5 minutes, then 10 minutes, then 15 minutes, then 20 minutes until your child is asleep.
sources.supports: Fear of the dark is normal in young children; skip monster spray and monster sweeping; check in at growing intervals (5, 10, 15, 20 minutes).

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital (clinical staff, updated 1 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... briefly checking in on them in their bed and reassuring them in 5 minutes, and then every 10 minutes until they are asleep. ... Avoid scary TV shows, videos, or stories that may add to your child's fears. ... a security object (like a small stuffed animal) they can keep in bed with them may be beneficial.
sources.supports: Nighttime fears are normal; do not dismiss them; a nightlight is fine; read stories about children who conquer fears; brief check-ins at 5 then 10 minutes; avoid scary media; a security object in bed.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds (Gene Beresin)
sources.quote: you can ask open ended questions like, 'What are you afraid of when you go to bed?' ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone. ... Use Books and Movies About Nighttime Fears.
sources.supports: Ask open questions about what scares the child at bedtime; praise brave steps; use books about nighttime fears.
